title: The RSI(2) pullback everyone quotes won 76% of its SPY trades since 2001 and still made less than half of what holding did
author: person-person12
selftext:
Larry Connors' RSI(2) rule gets passed around as the high win rate strategy that actually holds up, so I ran the textbook version on SPY daily candles from January 2001 to March 2026 in [Agenticks](https://www.agenticks.ca/?utm_source=reddit&utm_medium=post&utm_campaign=autopilot&utm_content=ai_trading). Buy the close when the 2 day RSI is under 10 and SPY is above its 200 day average, sell on the first close back above the 5 day average. No stop and no target, the full account goes into every trade, commission and slippage are charged on every fill, and both sides are price only with no dividends.

**RSI(2):** $10,000 became **$21,420**, 186 trades, 75.8% winners, profit factor 2.2, worst drawdown 14.9%.

**Holding SPY:** $10,000 became **$49,233**, worst drawdown 56.5%.

The win rate is real and most of the trades are out in under a week. What it costs you is time in the market. The 200 day filter kept it completely flat from October 2007 to June 2009, which is most of why the drawdown is so small, but the same filter plus the need for a sharp dip means it sat in cash through a lot of the years SPY just kept grinding up.

The worst single trade was the August 2011 downgrade, bought at $130.62 on July 28 and sold at $118.38 on August 12 for **-$1,272 on the account**. Covid caught it once too, in at $323.96 on February 25 2020 and out at $309.47 on March 3, and it didnt take another trade until September 2020.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
the comparison that's fair to it is return per day actually invested, because it's in the market a small fraction of the time. the honest read is that it's a cash-plus overlay rather than a replacement for holding, and the flat stretch through 2008 is the whole pitch.

one thing to check on the fill: buying the close of the signal bar is only possible if you compute the RSI a minute before the bell, otherwise the real entry is the next open, and on a two day RSI that gap matters.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body:
Yea **cash-plus overlay** is the right way to frame it, comparing it to buy and hold straight up is a bit unfair when its sitting out most of the time.

The fill point is fair too. Buying the close assumes you have the RSI a minute before the bell, and most ppl running this by hand dont, so the next open is the honest entry for them and on a 2 day RSI that gap eats into the edge.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: worth rerunning with next-open fills just to see how much of the 2.2 survives. my guess is most of it, the dips it buys rarely finish reverting overnight, but I've been wrong on exactly that kind of guess before.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Those fills are already the next open. It signals on the close and fills at the next days open, and **the 2.2 is after commission and slippage** on every trade, so your guess was right and that is what survives.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: ah, so the 2.2 is already the honest version. then it's a better result than I gave it credit for.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: yea for a rule that simple its a solid number. the catch is still the one in the title, it only owns SPY right after a dip so the money sits in cash between trades, and **over 25 years thats where holding pulls away**.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: The cash drag is the whole gap, the rule is in the market maybe a third of the time. The fair comparison would be per day invested rather than per calendar year, which I have not run yet.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea agreed, per day invested is the fairer way to line them up. The catch is that number quietly assumes the idle cash does something useful **the other two thirds of the time**, so id want it run with that cash sitting in t-bills before calling it better than just holding SPY.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: agreed, and I'd trust the t-bill version more. in the flat years the bill leg does most of the work, which is really the argument for calling it an overlay rather than a strategy.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: yea overlay is the right word for it tbh. the rule sits in cash most of the year, so whatever that cash is earning ends up **deciding a big chunk of the result** and the entry signal gets the credit for it.

comments.author: TopPromise9775
comments.body:
The idle cash and the missing dividends pull this comparison in opposite directions.



Because the strategy is out of the market most of the time, crediting idle cash with the contemporaneous 3-month Treasury rate could materially narrow the gap. But using SPY total return rather than price-only returns would widen it again.



I'd show both in a portfolio-level CAGR and Sharpe comparison, alongside exposure and return per invested day. That would separate whether the entry rule has an edge from whether sitting in cash was a good allocation decision.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Agreed. **Return per invested day answers whether the entry rule itself has an edge, while portfolio CAGR and Sharpe answer whether this was a worthwhile way to allocate the account.** The current comparison is price-only on both sides, so adding SPY total return and crediting cash at the contemporaneous 3-month Treasury rate is the clean rerun.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body:
Good breakdown, and agreed on where this needs to go next.

Worth being explicit about the three separate questions this compares, since they get conflated:

**1. Does the entry signal itself have edge?** That's answered by return per day invested, not total portfolio return. RSI(2) trades hold for roughly a week on average across 186 trades, so the capital is actually working for a small fraction of the \~9,100 trading days in the sample. Annualizing the per-trade return over invested days only (rather than calendar days) is the right way to isolate whether the 2-day RSI dip + 200-day filter combination is picking up real short-term mean reversion, separate from the fact that it's mostly sitting in cash. **2. Was this a good way to allocate the account?** That's CAGR and Sharpe on the full equity curve, cash included. And this is where crediting the idle cash at the contemporaneous 3-month T-bill rate matters a lot for a 2001–2026 sample — you're spanning a stretch that includes both near-zero rates and 5%+ short rates, so a flat 0% cash assumption understates the strategy's total return unevenly across different periods of the backtest. That alone could close a meaningful chunk of the gap versus buy-and-hold, though probably not all of it given the multi-year stretches the filter sits out entirely (like 2007–09 that you mention, but also several strong grinding-up years). **3. Is the comparison apples-to-apples?** Price-only on both sides undersells buy-and-hold specifically, since SPY's dividend yield compounds meaningfully over 25 years while the strategy's cash drag doesn't get any offsetting credit either. Total-return SPY vs. a rate-credited cash-plus-strategy equity curve is the fair version of this test.

If you want to actually run that rerun cleanly — total-return SPY, T-bill-credited cash, invested-day annualization, and Sharpe on both curves side by side — that's a pretty natural fit for something like EventTrader, since the whole point of that kind of engine is separating the signal's raw edge from the cash-drag/allocation question instead of eyeballing CAGR deltas. Would be curious to see the same 2001–2026 window rerun that way. [https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH](https://claude.ai/artifact/VuwYE2KYrtzMdwyEpvA9wH)

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: yea agreed, those get mashed together a lot. 186 trades at around a week each means it was only in SPY for a small slice of those 25 years, so **per day invested** it looks a lot better than the total does. the total is still what youd actually have in the account tho, and thats the number ppl skip when they quote the 76%

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Exactly right, and that's the actual takeaway worth stating plainly: win rate and per-trade stats sell the strategy, total account CAGR is what you'd actually have to show for it. Both numbers are true and neither is fake, they're just answering different questions — "is the signal real" vs. "should you have put your money here instead of just holding." The trap is that only the first one gets quoted because it's the more flattering one, not because it's more relevant to someone deciding what to actually do with their account.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: yea exactly, the win rate gets quoted because its the number that fits in a thumbnail. **total return next to just holding** is the one that tells you whether it was worth tying the account up at all.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Right, and that's really the whole tell for spotting a marketing page versus an honest one — if a strategy site leads with win rate and buries or omits the buy-and-hold comparison, that's not an oversight, it's a choice. The ones actually confident in the edge put CAGR-vs-benchmark front and center because it's the harder number to fake or cherry-pick around. Win rate alone can be dressed up all day with a tight stop and a wide target; total return next to a naive hold can't hide much.

replies.author: person-person12
replies.body: Yea exactly, a 76% win rate is about the easiest number there is to manufacture with a close target and a wide stop. **the hold figure is the one I want first** on any strategy page, which is why it sits right next to the result in every one of these I run.
